eras.label: The Radical republic
eras.blurb: The federal state born of the 1847 civil war elected its National Council in two-round district contests, and the victorious Radicals dominated it for seventy years — governing alone until 1891, when the first Catholic-Conservative joined the Federal Council. Elections were frequent, turnout modest, and the executive never once fell to them.

eras.label: The proportional turn
eras.blurb: The general strike of 1918 forced the change the Radicals had long resisted: proportional representation from 1919, which promptly cut their seats by half and made the Catholics and the new Farmers' Party permanent partners. The Socialists became the largest party in 1943 and joined the Federal Council that December, mid-war.

eras.label: The magic formula
eras.blurb: From 1959 the four governing parties split the seven Federal Council seats 2:2:2:1 by fixed convention, and elections became the world's most consequence-free: the same coalition governed regardless of the result. Turnout sagged below half. The formula held for forty-four years — until the SVP broke it.

eras.label: The SVP era
eras.blurb: Christoph Blocher turned a small agrarian party into the largest political force in Switzerland on an anti-EU, anti-immigration platform. The SVP claimed a second Federal Council seat in 2003, was briefly expelled from it, and set an all-time record of 62 National Council seats in 2023 — while the Greens' 2019 surge receded as fast as it came.

Federal elections were held in Switzerland on 19 October 2003. Although in Switzerland's political system, in which all four major parties form a coalition, it is very difficult to achieve a change of government, this election produced an upset with the strong showing of the right-wing, anti-European Union and anti-immigration Swiss People's Party.

Elections to the Swiss Federal Assembly, the federal parliament of Switzerland, were held on Sunday, 21 October 2007. In a few cantons, a second round of the elections to the Council of States was held on 11 November, 18 November, and 25 November 2007.

At the last election, in 2007, the Swiss People's Party (SVP) won the highest share of the vote ever recorded for a single party in Switzerland, with 29% of the vote. Soon after, a moderate faction split from the SVP, forming the Conservative Democratic Party (BDP).

Results showed a shift, due to voter concerns regarding refugee immigration, to the right and increased support for the three largest parties, with the strong showing of Swiss People's Party and FDP.The Liberals possibly affecting future reforms of energy, social security and tax issues, as well as the make-up of the seven-member government.

In the 20 October elections, the two green parties, the Green Party of Switzerland and the Green Liberal Party of Switzerland, made major electoral gains, taking 13.2% and 7.8% of the vote respectively. As in the previous election, the Swiss People's Party received the most votes, but its share of votes went down to 25.6% from 29.4%.

Federal elections were held in Switzerland on 22 October 2023 to elect all members of the National Council and Council of States. The elections were followed by elections to the Federal Council, Switzerland's government and collegial presidency, on 13 December.
